food.text: Ötzi, the natural mummy found in the Ötztal Alps, ate a last meal that included ibex meat and wheat grains. Scans showed his stomach had shifted upward after death, and the meat was confirmed by DNA analysis. He had eaten less than two hours before he died.

Ötzi, Europe's oldest known natural human mummy, was found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps on the Austria–Italy border. His stomach held the partly digested remains of ibex meat, confirmed by DNA analysis, and wheat grains. This suggests he ate a meal less than two hours before he died.

Los Millares, a Chalcolithic site near Almería in Spain, was in use from about 3025 BC and probably supported around 1,000 people. Although its inhabitants were primarily farmers, they had also learned to smelt and form copper. The site is important for understanding the shift from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age.

Analysis of Ötzi's intestines showed two meals, the last eaten about eight hours before his death. One was chamois meat and the other red deer and herb bread, both eaten with roots and fruits. The grain was highly processed einkorn wheat bran, possibly bread.

Ötzi's intestines showed two separate meals. The last one, eaten about eight hours before his death, was chamois meat. The other was red deer meat and herb bread, and both were eaten with roots and fruits.

The town of Los Millares had more than a thousand inhabitants. Its economy rested on copper metallurgy, agriculture, animal husbandry and hunting on a moderate scale. Its people also exported metal figures and pottery to a large part of the Iberian peninsula.

Near Ötzi's body, possibly from his provisions, researchers found chaff and grains of einkorn and barley. They also found seeds of flax and poppy, kernels of sloes and various wild berry seeds. Sloes are small plum-like fruits of the blackthorn tree.
The grain Ötzi ate with both of his last meals was a highly processed einkorn wheat bran, possibly made into bread.

A 2009 CAT scan revealed that Ötzi's stomach had shifted upward after death, to where his lower lung area would normally be. It is believed he most likely ate a few slices of dried, fatty meat from a wild goat in South Tyrol, Italy.

art.text: In the Côa Valley of northeastern Portugal, prehistoric people made open-air rock art that is carved, incised or picked into the stone, and only rarely painted. The artists used vertical schist slabs as their canvas.
art.source_title: Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde

art.text: Early farmers who arrived by sea decorated their pots by pressing shells of the genus Cardium into the clay. This Cardium pottery, also called Impressed Ware, spread along the coasts of the Western Mediterranean, from Liguria to southern France and Spain.

Statue menhirs, standing stones carved with human features and frequently depicting weapons, were first erected in northern Italy and Sardinia during the Copper Age. The sculptural tradition lasted in some regions well into the Bronze Age and even the Iron Age.

The carvings of the Côa Valley vary greatly in size, from 15 cm to 180 cm, though most are only 40 to 50 centimetres across. They often form panels and compositions, with bold lines that are sometimes touched with fine, thin ones.
art.source_title: Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde

art.text: Some engravings at Siega Verde are more recent, anthropomorphic figures dating to the Magdalenian age, about 9,000 years ago. Across the Siega Verde site there are 91 panels of engraved rock, spanning some 1 kilometre.
art.source_title: Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde

art.text: The cardial pottery culture, the main culture of the Mediterranean Neolithic, eventually stretched from the Adriatic Sea to the Atlantic coast of Portugal. It also reached south to Morocco, linking distant coasts through shared pottery decoration.

By the end of the sixth millennium BC, the Po Valley was a mosaic of cultures united by their pottery decoration. At the start of the fifth millennium BC this was replaced by the culture of the square mouthed vases, widespread from Liguria to Veneto.
Paintings at the Côa Valley from the Epipaleolithic period were zoomorphic and semi-naturalist in design. In the Neolithic, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic designs became geometric and abstract.
art.source_title: Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde

art.text: The tradition of statue menhirs in northern Italy and Sardinia may have come from the steppe, possibly from the Yamna culture. It proved remarkably durable, continuing in some regions into the Bronze Age and Iron Age.

Open-air rock art sites are rarer than cave sites, and few spread over 17 kilometres like the Côa Valley. Mazouco in Portugal and Siega Verde in Spain are similar open-air sites, and archaeologists regard such places as open-air sanctuaries of prehistoric hunter-gatherers.
art.source_title: Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde

art.text: Impressed pottery culture spread through southern Italy between the second half of the sixth millennium BC and the beginning of the fifth. It took hold especially in the Tavoliere delle Puglie, Irpinia and Basilicata, and from there moved north and along the Tyrrhenian coast.

war.text: Around 3025 BC, the settlement of Los Millares in southern Spain was ringed by three concentric lines of stone walls. The outer wall ran more than 200 meters and had 19 bastions and a gate guarded by forework. The site probably supported around 1,000 people.

Los Millares in southern Spain was ringed by three concentric lines of stone walls. The outer ring ran more than 200 meters and had 19 bastions, plus a gate guarded by foreworks. The settlement probably supported around 1,000 people.
The road leading to Los Millares was guarded by four smaller outlying stone forts. These stood in addition to the three rings of walls and the guarded gate of the main settlement.

An arrowhead was found embedded in the left shoulder of Ötzi, a man who lived during the 4th millennium BC, and a small matching tear was found in his coat. A 2001 X-ray and CT scan showed the arrowhead lodged in his shoulder when he died. Currently it is believed that Ötzi bled to death after the arrow shattered his scapula and damaged nerves and blood vessels before lodging near his lung. His body was found in the Ötztal Alps at the Austria–Italy border.

Los Millares, a Chalcolithic site in Andalucía, Spain, was protected by three concentric lines of stone walls. The outer ring ran more than 200 meters, with 19 bastions and a gate guarded by foreworks. The complex was in use from about 3025 BC.

Analysis of the grave goods and the cemetery of 70 tholos tombs at Los Millares led archaeologists to suggest its people lived in a stratified, unequal society. They believe it was often at war with its neighbors.
Beyond its three walls, Los Millares had four smaller outlying stone forts guarding the road that led to the site. This gave the settlement several layers of defense.

Radiocarbon dating shows that one wall at Los Millares collapsed and was rebuilt around 3025 BC. That is also roughly the date when the complex came into use, which means its defences needed major repair early in its history.

Ötzi was about 45 years old when he died around 3230 BCE. He stood about 160 cm tall and weighed an estimated 50 kg. Examination of his body found bruises and cuts to the hands, wrists and chest, cerebral trauma indicative of a blow to the head, and a cut at the base of his thumb that went to the bone and showed no scarring, suggesting it was fresh when he died. The circumstances of his death remain the subject of much investigation and speculation.

The road to Los Millares was guarded by four smaller outlying stone forts. Together with the walls and the guarded gate, they made the site a heavily defended place for its estimated 1,000 inhabitants.

The Remedello culture of the Po Valley in Northern Italy flourished during the Copper Age. Male graves held arrows, stone daggers and polished stone axes, and a few held axes and daggers or ornaments made of copper. Among its noteworthy finds are extremely accurate flint axes and other weapons, and objects in copper and arsenical silver that included arms.

Radiocarbon dating shows that one of the walls at Los Millares collapsed and was rebuilt around 3025 BC. The settlement's defenses were therefore kept in repair. Los Millares had been in use since about that date and lasted until about 2000 BC.

When Ötzi was removed from the ice on 23 September, a dagger was found beside him. A long wooden object nearby was later identified as a bow. No archaeologist was present at the removal, and several people had visited the site earlier, stepping on fragile objects and removing others before their locations were recorded. His body was damaged during recovery: a pneumatic drill damaged his hip, his left arm was broken during handling, and his longbow was broken.
Radiocarbon dating has established that one wall at Los Millares collapsed and was rebuilt around 3025 BC. The site's defenses were therefore repaired and maintained within its first years of use.

The Remedello culture takes its name from the town of Remedello in Brescia, where several burials were discovered in the late 19th century. The graves held a single body in a crouching or supine position, and male graves contained weapons such as arrows, stone daggers and polished stone axes. The weapons and other objects were characterized by decorative elements of eastern origin.

Archaeologist Konrad Spindler of the University of Innsbruck examined the find on 24 September. From the typology of an axe among the retrieved objects, he dated it to "at least four thousand years old". Later analysis showed the man lived between 3359 and 3105 BC.

science.text: Copper mining began in Liguria in the middle of the 4th millennium BC. The Libiola and Monte Loreto mines there are dated to 3700 BCE. They are the oldest copper mines in the western Mediterranean basin.

From the middle of the sixth millennium BC, Neolithic groups in Italy made wider use of local resources. They domesticated wild species such as cattle and pigs, and mixed farming with livestock in mostly permanent settlements. Mills, grinders and sickles show that agriculture was practised.
Neolithic influences from the east reached the Italian Peninsula around 6000 BCE and brought the Neolithic Revolution. The period lasted until about 3500-3000 BCE, when metallurgy began to spread.

The first wave of farming in the Western Mediterranean came by sea, carried by Cardium pottery. Its decoration was made by pressing the shells of the genus Cardium into the clay, which is why it is also called cardial ceramic. It appeared on coasts from Liguria to southern France and Spain.
The island of Lipari was colonized at the beginning of the fifth millennium BC by people coming from Sicily. They went there to exploit its deposits of obsidian.

In Sardinia, exploiting the obsidian deposits of Monte Arci led to the early development of Neolithic cultures. These were introduced with the culture of impressed pottery in the early sixth millennium BC.

The Remedello, Rinaldone and Gaudo cultures are late Neolithic cultures of Italy. Their traces are found mainly in Lombardy, Tuscany, Latium and Campania. They are sometimes called Eneolithic because they used primitive copper tools.

The main culture of the Mediterranean Neolithic is also called cardial ware. It eventually extended from the Adriatic Sea to the Atlantic coasts of Portugal, and south to Morocco. The more western Cardial style began in Provence, France, and reached western Portugal.
At the beginning of the fifth millennium BC, the mosaic of cultures in Northern Italy was replaced by the culture of the square mouthed vases. It was widespread from Liguria to Veneto.

culture.text: Around 6000 BCE, Neolithic influences reached the Italian Peninsula from the east, bringing the Neolithic Revolution. By roughly 3500 to 3000 BCE, metallurgy began to spread. This span shaped how early Italians lived, farmed and made things.

Early farmers in the western Mediterranean decorated their pottery by pressing the heart-shaped shell of the cockle Cerastoderma glaucum into wet clay. This style is called Cardium pottery, or Cardial ware, and it names the culture that made and spread it.

Northern Italy and Sardinia saw the earliest statue menhirs, which frequently depicted weapons. This sculptural tradition may have steppe origins in the Yamna culture. It lasted in some regions well into the Bronze Age and even the Iron Age.

The Gaudo culture of Campania is known almost exclusively through its tombs, active at the end of the 4th millennium BC. Its necropolis near Paestum covers about 2000 square metres and holds 34 separate tombs, each cut into the rock in an oven shape. Each tomb's one or two chambers held several human skeletons laid in the fetal position, on their sides or backs. The tombs were used repeatedly, and the most recently dead was always placed at the back of the chamber, with the earlier occupants beside him.

Ötzi, the Iceman, died around 3230 BCE in the Ötztal Alps on the Austria–Italy border. An arrowhead was lodged in his left shoulder, and it is currently believed he bled to death after the arrow shattered his scapula and damaged nerves and blood vessels before lodging near his lung. The arrow's shaft had been removed before death, and his body had bruises and cuts on the hands, wrists and chest, a cut to the bone at the base of his thumb, and cerebral trauma indicative of a blow to the head. Researchers therefore believe he was killed by another person.

Cardial pottery spread about 2,000 km from the gulf of Genoa to the estuary of the Mondego in probably no more than 100 to 200 years, around 5500 BC. Researchers suggest this was a seafaring expansion that planted colonies along the coast.

Cardial culture spread with astonishing speed. Secure radiocarbon dates from the gulf of Genoa to the estuary of the Mondego match those for Iberia at about 5500 cal BC, a distance of 2,000 km covered in probably no more than 100 to 200 years. This suggests a seafaring expansion that planted colonies along the coast.

The Neolithic economy in Italy was mixed. From the middle of the sixth millennium BC, people domesticated wild species such as cattle and pigs, and farmed with mills, grinders and sickles in mostly permanent settlements. Hunting, fishing and shellfishing remained important activities.

Around 3700 BCE, people in Liguria were mining copper at Libiola and Monte Loreto. These are the oldest copper mines in the western Mediterranean basin. The Copper Age arrived early in the Italian area, first appearing in Liguria.

Los Millares is the type site of the Chalcolithic Millaran culture. Its people were mainly farmers who had also learned to smelt and form copper. The Millaran culture eventually came to dominate the Iberian peninsula.

Impressed ware did not always use shells, since archaeologists note that impressions can also be made with sharp objects such as a nail or comb. Impressed pottery is much more widespread than the Cardial kind. The Italian zone reaching the Ligurian coast is covered by impressed ware, distinct from the more western Cardial style.

Obsidian shaped early island life in the Italian region. Sardinia's Monte Arci deposits led to the early development of its Neolithic cultures. Lipari was colonized at the beginning of the fifth millennium BC by people from Sicily seeking its obsidian.

The Gaudo necropolis was discovered late in 1943, when construction of the Gaudo Airfield during the Allied campaign in Italy unearthed some tombs. A British officer and archaeologist, Lieutenant John G. S. Brinson, excavated them scientifically. His notebook is now held in the National Archeological Museum of Naples.

Early Cardial pottery also appears in Sardinia during the Su Carroppu culture, in the low strata of Su Coloru cave around 6000 BC. The earliest date for such pottery in Italy comes from Coppa Nevigata on the Adriatic coast of southern Italy, perhaps as early as 6000 cal BC.

Gaudo objects were being recovered long before modern archaeology. In the 5th or 4th century BC, Greek settlers deposited flint daggers, probably from graves, in an ancient sanctuary at Paestum. In the 18th century, William Hamilton brought a flint dagger and a vase to England, where they are now in the British Museum.

Los Millares was a fortified site: three concentric lines of stone walls, the outer ring running more than 200 meters with 19 bastions and a gate guarded by foreworks, and four smaller stone forts guarding the road to it. Analysis of the occupation material and grave goods from its cemetery of 70 tholos tombs has led archaeologists to suggest that its people lived in a stratified, unequal society which was often at war with its neighbors. Radiocarbon dating shows one wall collapsed and was rebuilt around 3025 BC. The Los Millares civilisation was replaced around 1800 BC, with the arrival of Bronze by the El Argar civilisation.
